title: A surprise bill for every bet
allegory: Cross-entropy is like a bettor spreading chips across every horse and then paying a bill of -log(share of chips on the winner): all chips on the winner costs nothing, a thin share costs a lot, and none at all is unpayable.
map: the bill: -log(share of chips on the winner)
the loss for one token: -log p_y
all chips on the winner: bill 0; none on it: infinite bill
p_y = 1 gives loss 0; p_y → 0 gives loss → ∞
the average bill over a whole race day
mean cross-entropy over every token in the batch
credit: Checking that the loss at initialisation equals log(number of classes) is a habit from Andrej Karpathy's 'A Recipe for Training Neural Networks'.

chapters.name: How wrong, exactly?
chapters.note: right answer: 'cat' ... so how bad was my guess?

cap.1: A language model guesses the next word by spreading its belief over every word it knows. You need one number that says how bad that guess was.
cap.2: The model outputs one logit per vocabulary entry (50,257 for GPT-2). Accuracy only says right or wrong; training needs a smooth score of how much belief went to the truth.
cap.3: We want a differentiable score for a predicted distribution against one observed label: the negative log-likelihood of the target under softmax(logits).

cap.1: Picture a bettor spreading 100 chips across every horse. After the race you pay a bill based only on the share of chips you put on the winner.
cap.2: Cross-entropy is that bill: -log(p_correct). All chips on the winner costs 0. Half costs 0.69. One percent costs 4.6. None costs infinity.
cap.3: Loss = -log p_y, the surprisal of the observed token. It is a proper scoring rule: your expected bill is lowest when you report your true beliefs, so it rewards honest probabilities.

cap.1: You never need the shares themselves. The bill is every horse's pooled score minus the winner's own score. Raise the winner's score and the bill falls.
cap.2: From logits z: loss = logsumexp(z) - z[y]. That is why F.cross_entropy takes raw logits: it fuses log-softmax with picking the target, so never softmax first.
cap.3: Stable form: logsumexp(z) = m + log Σ exp(z - m), with m = max z. Softmax then log can underflow p to 0 and return inf; the fused version never forms p explicitly.

cap.1: The bill as the winner's share shrinks. Being fairly sure costs little; being confidently wrong costs a fortune. Zero belief in the truth is unpayable.
cap.2: Going from 10% to 1% on the truth costs as much extra as going from 100% to 10%. Confident mistakes are punished hardest, and that steepness is what drives learning.
cap.3: The gradient w.r.t. logits is softmax(z) - onehot(y): predicted minus true. Each wrong token is pushed down by its probability; the right one is pulled up by 1 - p_y.

chapters.name: Know the baseline
chapters.verdict: log(vocab size) is the bill for knowing nothing. Read every loss against it.

cap.1: The bill has landmarks. Guessing evenly across 50,257 tokens costs about 10.8 per token. A fresh model should start there; worse means something is broken.
cap.2: At init the output is near uniform, so loss ≈ log(50257) ≈ 10.8. Stuck above that, the model is worse than guessing: look for a broken residual or labels off by one.
cap.3: Baselines: log(d_vocab) for uniform; the unigram entropy (about 7.3 on TinyStories) for frequency-only. Align logits[:, :-1] with tokens[:, 1:] or you train on the wrong target.

chapters.name: Loss as a probe
chapters.title: Per-token loss: random tokens, then the same tokens again (schematic)

cap.1: Feed a model a random string of words, then the same string again. The bill stays high the first time and drops the second: the model copies from earlier.
cap.2: Read per token, cross-entropy is a diagnostic. In [1.2] the drop on the second copy of a repeated random sequence is the signature that an induction head exists.
cap.3: Random tokens are unpredictable on first sight; on the repeat the answer is in context, so loss collapses. Zero-ablate the heads responsible and second-half loss climbs back.

cap.1: This one number trains every language model you will meet, and read token by token it tells you what the model has figured out.
cap.2: Check the loss at step 0 equals log(number of classes), then read per-token loss to see where the model is sure and where it is lost.
cap.3: Loss changes are the currency of interpretability: ablate or patch a component and measure the change in cross-entropy, or in its task-specific cousin, the logit difference.

coda.title: Set the right answer's score, a rival's score and the vocabulary size, and read the bill

curves.label: bill for every possible right-answer logit

caption.1: Drag the right answer's score up: the bill falls toward 0. Push the rival above it: the bill climbs. Set both to 0 to see the guessing baseline.
caption.2: The gradient on the right logit is p - 1: near -1 when the model is badly wrong, near 0 once it is right, so the push fades by itself as the bet improves.
caption.3: Here loss = log(e^zc + e^zr + V - 2) - zc, with the other V - 2 logits at 0. Raising V lifts the 'knowing nothing' floor from log 2 towards log 50257 ≈ 10.8.

hamming.what: The average of -log(probability the model gave the right answer), computed straight from the logits.
hamming.when: Whenever a model outputs a distribution over classes or tokens and you train or measure it, which is every language model.
hamming.why: It punishes confident mistakes hardest, has the clean gradient 'predicted minus true', and read per token it doubles as a probe of what the model knows.

object.title: The surprise landscape
object.subtitle: The bill as a hillside over two scores: the right answer's and a rival's.

cap.1: The bill as a landscape. One direction raises the right answer's score, the other raises a rival's. High ground means a big bill.
cap.2: x: the correct logit. y: a rival's logit. One more token sits at 0. Height is the cross-entropy.
cap.3: Surface: logsumexp([x, y, 0]) - x. Convex in the logits, which is part of why it trains so reliably.

cap.1: The bead rolling downhill is learning: it raises the right answer's score and lowers the rival's at the same time.
cap.2: Gradient descent on logits: the gradient is predicted minus true, so the rival is pushed down and the target pulled up.
cap.3: ∂L/∂z = softmax(z) - onehot(y): the descent direction is fixed by the probability gap on each token.

cap.1: From above, the valley has no bottom. The bill keeps shrinking as the right score grows, so the push slows but never quite stops.
cap.2: Cross-entropy with hard labels is never exactly 0 at finite logits, so logits keep growing unless something like weight decay holds them back.
cap.3: The infimum 0 is approached only as z_y - max others → ∞; the gradient decays like 1 - p_y rather than vanishing at a finite point.

cap.1: Add ten thousand other words and the whole landscape rises: the right answer now has to out-score far more competitors.
cap.2: More tokens at logit 0 lift the floor: with no preference at all, the bill is log of the vocabulary size.
cap.3: Adding mass to the partition function raises logsumexp everywhere; the uniform baseline is log V, about 10.8 for GPT-2's 50,257 tokens.

predict.q: The model puts probability 0.01 on the correct token. Roughly what is the loss?
predict.why: -ln(0.01) ≈ 4.6. The bill grows with surprise, logarithmically.

predict.q: A freshly initialised model with GPT-2's 50,257 tokens should start with loss near?
Why pass logits, not probabilities, to F.cross_entropy?

options.t: It fuses log-softmax, which is numerically stable

predict.why: Softmax then log can underflow to log(0); logsumexp(z) - z_y straight from logits never does.

object.where: Any classifier or next-token model, and any time you measure how surprised a model is by text.
